question: What made you want to study Hospitality Management?
lookingFor: A genuine, specific reason rooted in real exposure to the industry, not a vague love of travel.

bullets: Point to a concrete moment or experience that sparked the interest
Show you understand hospitality is a business, not just a lifestyle
Connect the interest to what you want to learn or do next
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I worked weekends at a family friend's guesthouse from the age of sixteen, and I noticed how much thought went into things guests never consciously see, like how staff are scheduled around check-in rushes. That made me realise hospitality is really an operations and people problem dressed up as friendliness. I want to study it properly because I want to understand the business side, not just the service side, before I try to run something myself.

commonMistakes: Saying 'I love meeting new people' with nothing more specific
Talking only about liking to travel or stay in hotels as a guest
Treating the course as a fallback rather than a genuine choice
followUps: What surprised you most about that early experience?

question: Why do you want to study Hospitality Management at our institution specifically?
lookingFor: Evidence of real research into this course's structure, placements, or faculty, not generic praise.

bullets: Name a specific feature of the course, such as an industry placement year or a named module
Explain why that feature matters to your own goals
Show awareness of what sets this course apart from similar ones
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Your course has a mandatory paid placement year with partner hotel groups, which matters to me because I don't want to graduate having only read about revenue management, I want to have actually sat with a front office team during a busy season. I also looked at your food and beverage operations module, which goes further into cost control than most courses I compared it against. That combination of hands-on placement and a serious operations curriculum is exactly what I'm after.

commonMistakes: Praise that could apply to any hospitality course anywhere
Citing rankings instead of specific course content
Not knowing the difference between this course and a general tourism degree
followUps: What would you want to get out of the placement year specifically?

question: Was there a particular experience that first drew you toward hospitality as a career?
lookingFor: A specific, memorable moment that shows authentic curiosity about how service or operations work.

bullets: Describe one concrete moment rather than a vague general feeling
Explain what it revealed to you about the industry
Link it to how you've followed up on that curiosity since
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: We stayed at a small boutique hotel on a family trip where the manager remembered my sister's dietary restriction from a booking note and had already adjusted the breakfast without anyone asking. It stuck with me because it wasn't luck, it was a system working quietly in the background. Since then I've paid much closer attention to how hotels and restaurants organise themselves behind the scenes, and I did a short work experience week at a hotel to see it up close.

commonMistakes: Giving an answer that sounds rehearsed with no specific detail
Describing only the guest experience with no curiosity about how it was produced
Failing to connect the memory to any later action
followUps: What have you done since to explore that interest further?

question: Tell us about any part-time work, internship, or work experience you've had in hospitality or a related service role.
lookingFor: A real, specific experience with evidence of what you learned about the industry from it.

bullets: Name the role, setting, and how long you did it
Give a concrete task or moment, not just a job title
State a specific lesson about hospitality that experience taught you
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I worked front of house at a busy café for a year and a half, mostly weekend shifts. The hardest part was managing a queue during a rush while still making each customer feel like they weren't just a ticket number, which taught me that good service under pressure is really about pacing and reading people quickly. It's a small operation compared to a hotel, but it gave me a real feel for the rhythm of service work, which is why I want to study the larger-scale version of it properly.

commonMistakes: Claiming experience with no concrete detail to back it up
Only describing duties with no reflection on what was learned
Dismissing unrelated part-time jobs as irrelevant when the transferable skills matter
followUps: What would you do differently if you were managing that shift yourself?

question: Have you read anything, or followed any source, that's shaped how you think about the hospitality industry?
lookingFor: Genuine engagement with the industry beyond the course brochure, and an ability to discuss it critically.

bullets: Name a specific book, publication, podcast, or report
Summarise one idea from it accurately and briefly
Give your own view on that idea rather than just repeating it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've been following Skift's coverage of the industry, and a piece on the rise of 'bleisure' travel, people extending business trips into leisure time, stuck with me. It made me think about how hotels are having to redesign their offer around guests who don't fit the old business-versus-holiday split cleanly. I'm not sure every property can chase that trend without losing focus, which is something I'd like to explore more in the course.

commonMistakes: Naming a source but being unable to say anything specific about its content
Only citing something generic like 'the news'
Repeating an idea with no personal opinion attached
followUps: Do you think that trend applies equally to smaller independent properties?

question: Can you explain what RevPAR is and why hotels track it?
lookingFor: A correct, clear explanation of the metric and an understanding of why it matters more than occupancy alone.

bullets: Define RevPAR correctly as revenue per available room
Explain it's occupancy rate multiplied by average daily rate
Explain why it matters more than tracking occupancy or rate alone
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: RevPAR stands for revenue per available room, and it's calculated by multiplying your occupancy rate by your average daily rate, or equivalently dividing total room revenue by total rooms available. Hotels track it because occupancy alone can be misleading, you could be fully booked but at rock-bottom prices and still be losing money compared to a competitor. RevPAR captures both how full you are and how much you're actually earning per room, which is why it's the standard way properties compare performance against each other.

commonMistakes: Confusing RevPAR with average daily rate alone
Getting the formula backwards or inventing one
Not being able to explain why it matters beyond reciting the definition
followUps: If occupancy goes up but RevPAR goes down, what might that tell you?

question: How do hotel star ratings actually work, and what do they tell a guest?
lookingFor: Basic accurate knowledge that ratings reflect facilities and service standards, and awareness that they vary by country and aren't perfectly consistent.

bullets: Explain that ratings reflect facilities, services, and standards, not just luxury
Note that ratings are assessed by different bodies depending on the country
Show awareness that a rating doesn't guarantee consistency or a good guest experience
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Star ratings are meant to signal a certain level of facilities and service, things like room size, whether there's twenty-four hour reception, or restaurant options, and they usually range from one to five stars. What I find interesting is that the system isn't global, a national tourism board or private inspection body assesses hotels differently depending on the country, so a four-star hotel in one place isn't guaranteed to match one elsewhere. It's a useful shorthand for guests, but I don't think it always captures things like genuine service quality, which is where reviews fill the gap.

commonMistakes: Assuming stars measure luxury alone rather than facilities and standards
Assuming the system is identical and universally regulated everywhere
Confusing star ratings with guest review scores
followUps: Why might a guest trust online reviews over the official star rating?

question: A guest is furious that their room isn't ready two hours after the promised check-in time. How would you handle it?
lookingFor: A calm, structured approach that prioritises listening and a genuine fix over scripted apologies.

bullets: Acknowledge the guest's frustration genuinely before explaining anything
Offer a concrete interim solution, not just an apology
Follow through and check back once the issue is resolved
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd start by actually listening rather than jumping straight into an explanation, because right then the guest wants to feel heard more than they want an excuse. I'd apologise sincerely, explain briefly what's causing the delay, and offer something concrete in the meantime, like storing their luggage, a voucher for the lounge, or a complimentary drink while they wait. Once the room is ready I'd follow up personally rather than leaving it to whoever's on shift, because closing the loop is what actually turns a bad first impression around.

commonMistakes: Jumping to excuses before acknowledging the guest's frustration
Offering only an apology with no concrete gesture
Treating the interaction as over once the room is ready, with no follow-up
followUps: What would you do if the guest demanded a full refund on the spot?

question: In your own words, what separates good customer service from great customer service in hospitality?
lookingFor: A thoughtful distinction beyond 'being nice', ideally touching on anticipation and personalisation.

bullets: Distinguish reactive service (fixing problems) from proactive service (anticipating needs)
Give a concrete example to illustrate the difference
Show understanding that consistency matters as much as individual moments
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Good service is doing what's asked competently and politely, but great service is noticing what wasn't asked. It's the difference between fixing a problem well when a guest complains and never letting the problem happen because staff were watching for it. I saw this at a restaurant where the server noticed a couple's phone was low on charge and quietly brought a charger without being asked. That kind of attentiveness is hard to script, which is exactly why I think staff culture matters as much as training manuals.

commonMistakes: Giving only 'being friendly' as the answer
Describing service with no concrete example
Confusing luxury amenities with actual service quality
followUps: Can great service exist without the physical facilities to back it up?

question: What do you think is the biggest challenge facing the hospitality industry right now?
lookingFor: A current, informed view backed by reasoning, showing the applicant follows the industry beyond the classroom.

bullets: Name a specific, real challenge rather than something vague like 'competition'
Explain why it matters with some reasoning or evidence
Show awareness of how the industry is responding to it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think staffing is the biggest one. A lot of hotels and restaurants are still struggling to fill front-line roles after the pandemic pushed people out of the industry, and that shortage puts pressure on service quality exactly where guests notice it most. What interests me is how properties are responding, some are investing in better pay and career pathways to make the industry more attractive again, while others are leaning on technology like self-check-in to reduce how many staff they need in the first place. I think the first approach is more sustainable long term.

commonMistakes: Naming something too vague to discuss further, like 'competition'
Picking a challenge with no supporting reasoning
Showing no awareness of how the industry is actually responding
followUps: Do you think technology is a real solution to that problem, or just a workaround?

subtopic: Front of house vs back of house
question: What's the difference between front-of-house and back-of-house operations in a hotel, and why does the distinction matter?
lookingFor: A clear, accurate explanation with awareness that the two must coordinate closely even though guests only see one side.

bullets: Define front-of-house as guest-facing roles like reception, concierge, and dining service
Define back-of-house as unseen operations like housekeeping coordination, kitchen, and maintenance
Explain why coordination between the two determines the guest experience
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Front-of-house covers everything a guest directly interacts with, reception, concierge, servers in the restaurant, while back-of-house covers the operations that support it but stay out of sight, like the kitchen, housekeeping, and maintenance. The distinction matters because a guest's experience actually depends on both working in sync, if housekeeping falls behind schedule, front desk staff end up apologising for something they didn't cause. I think that's why cross-department communication is such a big deal in hospitality management, the guest never sees the handoff, they only see whether it worked.

commonMistakes: Only describing front-of-house and forgetting back-of-house entirely
Treating the two as unrelated departments rather than interdependent
Giving examples that don't actually fit the category named
followUps: Which side would you rather start your career in, and why?

question: Where do you see yourself in the hospitality industry in ten years, and how does this course get you there?
lookingFor: An ambitious but realistic direction, clearly linked to what the course actually offers.

bullets: Give a direction rather than an overly specific job title
Connect it honestly to what the course provides
Show openness to how the path might change along the way
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd like to be running operations for a boutique hotel group, somewhere that cares as much about the guest experience as the numbers behind it. I know the exact title might look different by the time I get there, and that's fine. What I'm confident about is that this course's mix of operations, finance, and people management modules gives me the grounding to move up through different departments and actually understand the whole business rather than staying in one lane.

commonMistakes: An overly rehearsed, unrealistically specific plan
A goal with no real connection to what the course offers
Sounding uncertain about staying in the industry at all
followUps: What's the first job you'd want after graduating?

question: How do you think hotels can balance sustainability with the guest experience they promise?
lookingFor: Awareness that sustainability and guest comfort aren't automatically in tension, with a specific example.

bullets: Give a concrete example of a sustainability measure hotels use
Address the perceived tension with guest comfort or luxury
Show a balanced, realistic view rather than pure idealism or cynicism
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A lot of people assume sustainability means asking guests to sacrifice comfort, like reusing towels, but I think the more interesting shift is happening behind the scenes where guests don't even notice, things like smart heating systems that only run in occupied rooms or sourcing food locally to cut transport emissions. Done well, it can actually improve the experience rather than diminish it, fresher food is a guest benefit, not just an environmental one. The tension only really shows up when sustainability is used as a cost-cutting excuse dressed up as a green initiative, and I think guests can usually tell the difference.

commonMistakes: Assuming sustainability always means guest sacrifice
Giving only vague ideas like 'going green' with no specifics
Ignoring the cost or operational trade-offs involved
followUps: Can you think of a sustainability measure that guests might actually resent?

question: Hotels sometimes deliberately overbook rooms, expecting some guests to cancel or not show up. Do you think this practice is ethical?
lookingFor: Structured reasoning that weighs business logic against guest harm, not a snap judgment either way.

bullets: Explain the business logic behind overbooking honestly
Weigh it against the real harm caused when it goes wrong
Land on a nuanced position, such as it being defensible only with a strong contingency plan for displaced guests
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I understand why hotels do it, no-shows and late cancellations are real and predictable enough that overbooking by a small margin protects revenue that would otherwise be lost. But I don't think that makes it automatically fine, because when the maths gets it wrong, an actual guest is left without the room they booked and paid for, sometimes arriving after a long journey. I'd say it's ethically defensible only if the hotel has a genuine plan for that scenario, comparable alternative accommodation, transport, and real compensation, rather than treating the walked guest as an unfortunate rounding error. Without that safety net, it's really just shifting risk onto the person least able to absorb it.

commonMistakes: Condemning the practice outright with no understanding of the business logic
Defending it purely on revenue grounds with no concern for guest harm
Refusing to take a clear position at all
followUps: How would you personally handle telling a guest they've been walked to another hotel?

question: Why is teamwork across different departments, like housekeeping, front desk, and food and beverage, so important in a hotel?
lookingFor: Understanding that guest experience depends on coordination across departments that rarely interact directly with each other.

bullets: Explain that departments operate somewhat independently but affect the same guest
Give a concrete example of what goes wrong when coordination fails
Note that communication systems, not just goodwill, make this work
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A guest doesn't experience a hotel department by department, they experience one continuous stay, so if housekeeping and front desk aren't talking to each other, a guest can be checked into a room that isn't actually ready. I saw something similar working at a café, where the kitchen and the floor staff not communicating about a delay meant customers got told conflicting things by different people. In a hotel that kind of gap is worse because it's not just annoying, it can mean broken promises about check-in time or dietary needs. That's why I think the systems hotels use to pass information between departments matter as much as the individual staff being good at their jobs.

commonMistakes: Giving only a generic 'teamwork is important' answer
Naming departments with no example of what breaks without coordination
Overlooking the role of communication systems and only focusing on personalities
followUps: What tools or systems have you seen used to keep departments in sync?

question: Is there a hospitality brand or company you admire? What do they do well, and where do you think they fall short?
lookingFor: A specific, balanced view of a real company showing genuine industry knowledge rather than pure brand loyalty.

bullets: Name a specific company and what they actually do differently
Give a genuine limitation or criticism, not just praise
Show this comes from real observation, not marketing copy
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I admire what Ace Hotel has done with turning hotels into local cultural hubs, their lobbies double as coworking spaces and event venues that locals actually use, not just guests, which builds a kind of loyalty that a standard chain struggles to match. Where I think they fall short is consistency, because that identity depends heavily on the specific city and building, so the experience can vary a lot between properties in a way a more standardised chain wouldn't. I find that trade-off genuinely interesting, between character and consistency, and it's something I'd like to understand better through the course.

commonMistakes: Only praising the brand with no honest limitation
Naming a brand but being unable to say anything specific about it
Reciting the company's own marketing language as if it were analysis
followUps: Would you rather work for a large chain or an independent property, and why?

question: How is technology changing the way hotels operate, and do you think it always improves the guest experience?
lookingFor: Concrete examples of hospitality technology plus a balanced view of its trade-offs.

bullets: Give a specific example, such as property management systems, mobile check-in, or dynamic pricing tools
Explain what benefit that technology actually provides
Give a genuine limitation or downside, showing balanced thinking
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Property management systems have changed a lot behind the scenes, they connect reservations, housekeeping status, and billing so staff aren't relying on separate spreadsheets or phone calls between departments. On the guest-facing side, mobile check-in and keyless entry save time and appeal to guests who want minimal contact. But I don't think it always improves the experience, some guests specifically choose hospitality over an Airbnb because they want a human interaction at the desk, and stripping that out in the name of efficiency can undercut the whole point of the stay. I think the best use of technology removes friction from the boring parts, not the human parts.

commonMistakes: Naming technology with no explanation of how it actually helps
Assuming more technology is automatically better
Giving no concrete example, only speaking in generalities
followUps: Can you think of a guest situation where you'd deliberately avoid using technology?

question: How would you make sure guests from very different cultural backgrounds all feel genuinely welcome?
lookingFor: Awareness that hospitality is not one-size-fits-all, with practical thinking rather than vague statements about respect.

bullets: Show awareness that expectations around service, privacy, or dining vary by culture
Give a concrete practical example of adapting service accordingly
Balance adapting to differences with treating every guest as an individual, not a stereotype
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd want staff to understand that what feels like good service isn't universal, some guests expect a lot of personal attention and small talk, while others find that intrusive and would rather be left alone. I've read about hotels training staff on things like appropriate greeting distance or dietary and religious considerations around meal times, which are practical rather than symbolic gestures. At the same time I think it's important not to assume everyone from one background wants the same thing, so genuinely asking and paying attention to the individual guest in front of you matters more than following a checklist by nationality.

commonMistakes: Answering only with 'treat everyone the same' which misses genuine cultural differences
Relying on broad stereotypes about what a nationality wants
Giving no practical example of how service would actually adapt
followUps: How would you train a team to get this right without relying on stereotypes?

question: How would you explain the difference between hospitality management and tourism management to someone unfamiliar with either?
lookingFor: A clear, accurate distinction showing the applicant genuinely understands what they're applying for, not just the general field.

bullets: Explain hospitality management focuses on running the operations of places people stay, eat, or are hosted
Explain tourism management focuses more broadly on travel, destinations, and visitor movement
Note that the two overlap but are distinct fields of study and career paths
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Hospitality management is really about the operational side of running the businesses that host people, hotels, restaurants, event venues, everything from staffing to service standards to revenue. Tourism management sits a level up from that, it's more about why and how people travel, destination marketing, and the wider visitor economy, which can include transport and attractions that have nothing to do with accommodation. They obviously connect, a destination's tourism appeal drives demand for hospitality businesses, but I chose hospitality specifically because I'm more drawn to the operations and people side than to destination-level strategy.

commonMistakes: Treating the two fields as identical
Being unable to explain the distinction at all
Describing hospitality management as only hotels and ignoring restaurants or events
followUps: Which part of hospitality operations interests you most, rooms, food and beverage, or events?

question: It's the busiest night of the year, two staff have called in sick, and the kitchen is falling behind. As the shift supervisor, what do you do?
lookingFor: Calm prioritisation, clear communication, and realistic decision-making under pressure, not a fantasy of doing everything perfectly.

bullets: Prioritise quickly rather than trying to fix everything at once
Communicate honestly with both the team and affected guests
Make a realistic trade-off, such as adjusting expectations rather than pretending nothing is wrong
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: First I'd figure out where the bottleneck actually is rather than reacting to every complaint at once, if it's the kitchen falling behind, I'd see whether front of house can slow the pace of new orders and be upfront with tables about a longer wait rather than letting them sit confused. I'd redeploy whoever I can spare to the busiest point, even if that means I'm running food myself for a while. I'd also tell the team honestly that it's going to be a hard night and thank them for pushing through it, because morale matters as much as logistics when everyone's stretched. Afterward I'd want to understand why we were short-staffed in the first place so it's not a repeat problem.

commonMistakes: Claiming to fix every problem simultaneously with no real prioritisation
Ignoring communication with guests about the delay
Not reflecting on the underlying staffing issue at all
followUps: How would you handle a guest who refuses to accept the delay and demands to leave without paying?

question: Why might a hotel charge a different price for the exact same room on two different nights?
lookingFor: Understanding of dynamic pricing driven by demand, and the reasoning behind it, not just 'because they can'.

bullets: Explain that pricing responds to demand, such as events, seasonality, or day of week
Note that a room sold is perishable inventory, an empty room tonight earns nothing back tomorrow
Show understanding that this is a deliberate revenue management strategy, not random
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A hotel room is what's sometimes called perishable inventory, if it isn't sold tonight, that revenue is gone forever, you can't sell yesterday's room tomorrow. That's why hotels adjust prices based on expected demand, a night during a local festival or conference will be priced far higher than a quiet midweek night, because the hotel knows it can fill rooms either way and wants to capture the extra willingness to pay when demand is strong. On slow nights, lowering the price to fill rooms that would otherwise sit empty still contributes to covering fixed costs like staffing and utilities, even at a lower margin. It's essentially the same logic airlines use for flight tickets.

commonMistakes: Explaining it as simply 'greed' with no underlying business logic
Not mentioning that unsold rooms represent permanently lost revenue
Confusing dynamic pricing with unrelated concepts like loyalty discounts
followUps: Is there a risk in pricing too aggressively during high-demand periods?

subtopic: Why a degree rather than straight into the industry
question: Hospitality is an industry where a lot of people rise without a degree. Why do you want to study it formally rather than just starting work?
lookingFor: A genuine reason for choosing structured study, showing understanding of what a degree adds beyond on-the-job learning.

bullets: Acknowledge honestly that experience alone can and does work in this industry
Explain specifically what structured study adds, such as breadth across departments or business fundamentals
Show the two aren't mutually exclusive, and that you intend to combine study with real experience
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I know plenty of people build strong careers in hospitality by working their way up, and I don't think a degree is the only path. What draws me to studying it formally is the breadth, on the job you tend to learn deeply about the one department you're in, but a degree exposes me to finance, marketing, and operations across the whole business before I specialise, which I think makes for a better general manager down the line. I'm not choosing study instead of experience though, that's exactly why the placement year matters to me, I want both.

commonMistakes: Dismissing the value of hands-on experience entirely
Being unable to say what a degree adds beyond a job title
Suggesting the degree is only about credentialing, not learning
followUps: What's one thing you think you can only learn on the job, not in a classroom?

question: What do you think is the biggest operational difference between running a luxury hotel and a budget hotel?
lookingFor: Understanding that the difference is about business model and guest expectations, not just price or decor.

bullets: Identify a real operational difference, such as staffing ratio or personalisation versus standardisation
Connect it to the different guest expectations each segment serves
Avoid implying one model is simply worse or lower quality
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think the biggest difference is the staff-to-guest ratio and how much personalisation is built into the model. A luxury property is often selling the relationship itself, staff remembering preferences, anticipating needs, which requires far more staff hours per guest. A budget hotel is usually selling reliability and value at scale, so the operational focus is on standardising processes so quality doesn't depend on any one staff member's memory or judgement. Neither model is worse, they're just answering different questions about what the guest actually wants from the stay.

commonMistakes: Reducing the difference to just 'luxury has nicer furniture'
Implying budget hospitality is a lesser or lower-effort business
Giving no operational detail, only describing guest perception
followUps: Which segment would you rather start your career in, and why?

question: What's a trend in travel or hospitality you find genuinely interesting, and why?
lookingFor: A specific, current trend discussed with genuine curiosity and some critical thinking about its implications.

bullets: Name a specific, current trend rather than something generic
Explain why it's happening, not just that it's happening
Offer a view on where it might be heading or its limitations
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'm interested in the growth of wellness-focused travel, where the trip itself is built around something like sleep retreats or digital detox programmes rather than sightseeing. I think it's happening because a lot of people's default state now is being constantly reachable, so a holiday that actively removes that has become valuable in a way it wasn't a decade ago. What I wonder about is whether it can scale beyond a niche premium market, because a lot of what makes those retreats work, like genuine isolation, becomes harder to deliver as the concept gets copied more widely.

commonMistakes: Naming a trend with no explanation of the underlying cause
Choosing something too vague, like 'people want unique experiences'
Offering no critical view, only enthusiasm
followUps: How do you think a traditional hotel could adapt to that trend without losing its core identity?

question: What personal quality do you have that you think makes you well suited to a career in hospitality?
lookingFor: Genuine self-awareness backed by a specific example, not a generic trait with no evidence.

bullets: Name one specific trait rather than a long list
Back it with a concrete example that demonstrates it
Connect it honestly to what hospitality actually requires day to day
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd say it's staying calm and reading a situation quickly under pressure. Working at the café during the lunch rush, I learned to notice which customer was getting impatient versus which one just looked tired, and adjust how I approached each one without them ever seeing me stressed. Hospitality runs on exactly that kind of split-second judgement multiplied across a whole floor, and I think it's a trait you either build through real practice or you don't have it yet, which is part of why I want more of that experience through this course.

commonMistakes: Naming a generic trait like 'friendly' with no supporting example
Listing too many qualities instead of one well-argued one
Choosing a trait that doesn't actually connect to hospitality work
followUps: Tell us about a specific moment that trait was tested.
